slides.title: Ch. 22: Recognizing Text
slides.sub: Text in images: OCR with Tesseract and pytesseract, searchable PDFs and the screen

items.body: Every output on these slides was printed by the Python above when the deck was made, and every picture was saved by a program that is run again to check it. Windows, macOS, a scanner and a real screen were never used: the screen program ran on a virtual display, and what could not be run is marked on its slide.

slides.notes: Chapter 21 taught a program to make pictures. Chapter 22 teaches a program to read them: Tesseract, an open-source engine that turns the letters of an image into text, and pytesseract, the Python wrapper that calls it. The chapter has 8 listings and 2 figures, and ends with 7 practice questions and 1 practice program, the Browser Text Scraper. This deck follows the chapter in its own order: reading an image in four lines, the mistakes in the result, preparing an image before it is read, other languages, a searchable PDF made with the NAPS2 application run from Python, and reading the screen. It adds what the research found when every printed output was run again: Appendix A pins pytesseract 0.3.10, which cannot even be imported on Python 3.14; the first word of the book's Figure 22-1 is Iv in the book and In with the Tesseract of Ubuntu, because the engine, its data and its version all change the answer; the chapter's advice on small, tilted and noisy pages is true, and the deck puts numbers on it; the language codes are not all what the chapter calls them; NAPS2 refuses to overwrite a file and still returns 0; and the shipped preprocessing script calls names it never defines. The output of this chapter is text from a picture, so the deck shows the picture next to the text: fourteen pictures that programs saved are on the slides as images, and each caption names the program that made the picture. The build runs every such program again and refuses the deck unless the slide holds a picture that is byte for byte, or pixel for pixel, what the program saves now. Every output on the slides was printed by Python 3.14.6, installed with uv, with pytesseract 0.3.13, Pillow 12.3.0, NumPy 2.5.4, OpenCV 5.0.0.93, PyAutoGUI 0.9.54 and the Tesseract 5.3.4 of Ubuntu 24.04. Windows and macOS were never used, no scanner was attached, and nobody looked at a real screen: the screen program ran on a virtual display, which the slide says. What could not be run is marked on its slide.

slides.notes: The route has six parts. It starts with reading an image: what a program can ask Tesseract for, the four lines of the chapter, and the same page read by different engines with a different first word. Then the installation and what pytesseract does: the pins of Appendix A run on Python 3.14, how the wrapper talks to the engine, and the words, boxes and confidence of image_to_data(). The third part is accuracy and preparing an image: what hurts, cleaning a page, straightening and denoising with OpenCV, segmentation modes, hyphens and look-alike digits, and the mistakes a spell checker cannot see. The fourth is languages, data files and engines. The fifth is searchable PDFs, the screen and the releases: NAPS2, its overwrite rule and page slices, the other routes to a PDF, reading the screen, and the nine configurations of the research. The last part is a one-map summary and the resources. The ranges name the exact slides, so you can return to the part you need. Four of the six stories are on slides, each with a link, and two, Emanuel Goldberg's Statistical Machine and Kurzweil's reading machine, are told in the notes; the eight narrative diagrams of the chapter are drawn from the same specifications as the interactive page. Every output was printed by Python 3.14.6 with pytesseract 0.3.13, Pillow 12.3.0 and the Tesseract 5.3.4 of Ubuntu, the screen program ran on a virtual display, and what could not be run is marked on its slide.

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.sub: The chapter's own competency questions; the summary comes back to each

items: Which parts of a program that reads text from pictures can be shown to work, and which can only be shown to fail, on a machine that has no scanner, no real screen and no Windows or macOS, and how large is the spread between engine versions and data files?

Which printed outputs, programs, numbers and statements of the chapter differ in current releases of Python, pytesseract, Pillow and Tesseract, with the versions its appendix pins, with the data files installed, or in the files and pages it points to, and on what source?

slides.notes: The first question is the spine of the chapter, and the deck answers it slide by slide. On a machine with no scanner and no screen, a program can read a picture, give back the words, their boxes and a confidence for each, and make a searchable PDF, and the result can be compared with the text that was printed on the page; that is what can be shown to work. What can only be shown to fail is the part that needs a person's machine: the Windows and macOS installers, the Flatpak of NAPS2, a scanner, a large language model and a real screen. The research used a virtual X display, Xvfb, with the real ImageMagick display and PyAutoGUI, and took a screenshot of that screen; nobody looked at a real monitor, and the deck says so where it comes up. The second question is the watch-out. The chapter's 22 statements that can be replayed were run as printed in nine configurations: with the Tesseract 5.3.4 of Ubuntu and its fast English data 18 of 22 matched the book; with 5.5.3 and the fast data 20, with 5.5.3 and the best data 18, with 4.1.1 and the fast data 20, with all the apt languages 19 and with all languages under 5.5.3 21; with the book's pins, 18 on Python 3.13.14, 8 on Python 3.14.6, and 0 in an empty Python. The statements that still differ are get_languages(), the first word Iv of Figure 22-1, the Japanese heading and the English gibberish read from the Japanese page. The online materials of the book, 91 files, hold the four files of this chapter and not the others the chapter creates or assumes. Each slide says where a printed line differs and on what evidence.

items.who: Hyman Eli Goldberg, who was granted the patent, and Edmund Fournier d'Albe, who developed the Optophone
items.where: The patent is US Patent 1165663; the Optophone was a handheld scanner moved across a printed page

slides.notes: Wikipedia's article on optical character recognition says its roots lie in telegraphy and in reading devices for the blind. In 1915 Hyman Eli Goldberg was granted a patent for a device that read perforated or conductive-ink characters and converted them into standard telegraph code. Concurrently Edmund Fournier d'Albe developed the Optophone, a handheld scanner that produced tones corresponding to specific letters when it was moved across a printed page. In this study pytesseract returned the string 'Tesseract reads this line of text' with a newline at its end for a line the program drew, a str and not a tone or a code. The account rests on these sources. Wikipedia, 'Optical character recognition' (Hyman Eli Goldberg's patent of 1915, US Patent 1165663; the Optophone of Edmund Fournier d'Albe), read 2026-10-13; this study's leaves ImageToString and ReturnType. The use-case diagram lists what the wrapper can return: the text with image_to_string(), the words with their boxes and confidence with image_to_data(), a searchable PDF with image_to_pdf_or_hocr(), the orientation of a page with image_to_osd(), the installed languages with get_languages(), and the engine version with get_tesseract_version(). They are independent calls to one program, which is why the picture is a set of uses and not a sequence. The chapter's page was read on 13 October 2026; it returned 200 with 40,521 bytes and holds 8 listings and 2 figures, and its SHA-256 equals the digest that the book's own chapter ontology records. The card records what the research found on that day and this deck does not run again: the online materials of the third edition, a zip of 91 files, hold ocr-example.png of 939 by 1198 pixels in mode RGBA, frankenstein.png of 1130 by 672 pixels in mode P, frankenstein_jpn.png of 1211 by 606 pixels in mode RGB and preprocess_ocr.py of 190 lines; they hold none of ocrscreen.py, output.pdf, cat.png, dog.png, moose.png, spam.pdf, eggs.pdf or output.txt, which the chapter creates or assumes, and the publisher's book page has one occurrence of Recognizing Text and none of Tesseract, OCR or NAPS2. The deck downloads the zip while it runs and checks the SHA-256 of each file it uses; the book's scans are the book's own examples, and the study did not check their licence, so they are used here for teaching only. Two more stories of the study, Emanuel Goldberg and his Statistical Machine of 1931 and Ray Kurzweil's reading machine of 1976, are told in the notes of the slides on PDFs and on the sizes of letters: Wikipedia's article on Emanuel Goldberg says he introduced his "Statistical Machine", a document search engine that used photoelectric cells and pattern recognition to search the metadata on rolls of microfilmed documents. The patent, US 1,838,389, is dated 29 December 1931, and the article says the technology was used in a variant form in 1938 by Vannevar Bush in his microfilm rapid selector. A picture of a page is only searchable once something has read it. In this study a PDF that Pillow made from frankenstein.png held 0 characters of text for pdftotext, while the PDF that Tesseract made through pytesseract held 578 characters in 106 word boxes. Wikipedia's article on Kurzweil Computer Products says that in 1974 Ray Kurzweil founded the company and led development of the first omni-font optical character recognition system, a program able to recognize text in any normal font, where scanners before could read only a few fonts. The article on OCR gives 13 January 1976 as the day the finished reading machine for blind people was unveiled at a news conference. He later sold the company to Xerox. In this study six typefaces (DejaVu Sans, Serif, Mono and Bold, Nimbus Roman and Z003 italic script) drawn at 24 pixels were read with character error rates from 0.0 to 0.0116, and the same text drawn at 8 pixels with 0.2394.

items.who: Mary Shelley, whose name appeared on the revised edition of 1831 of a novel first published anonymously in 1818
items.where: London; the 1831 text had stylistic revisions and a new preface, and the chapter scans a page of that print

slides.notes: Wikipedia's article on Frankenstein says the novel was first published anonymously on 1 January 1818 and that in 1831 a revised edition was published under Mary Shelley's name. The 1831 version included significant stylistic revisions and a new preface, and chapter 22 of the book scans a page of that print, whose paper is wrinkled and yellowed. The book prints 'Iv' for the first word of the chapter. In this study Tesseract 5.3.4 returned 'In' for it, 4.1.1 and 5.5.3 with the fast data 'Iv', and the 106 words came back with 2 wrong, a character error rate of 0.0035. The account rests on these sources. Wikipedia, 'Frankenstein' (first published anonymously in 1818; the revised edition of 1831 under Mary Shelley's name), read 2026-10-13; this study's leaves FrankensteinOutput and ExactResultsVary. The page is Figure 22-1 of the book, frankenstein.png of the online materials, 1130 by 672 pixels in mode P. Tesseract 5.3.4 with the fast data returned 581 characters, and the book prints Iv as the first word of the sentence where this engine returns In; the picture shows the capital I followed by a small capital T, and the text of the page is IT was on a dreary night of November. Two words of the 106 differ from the printed page: IT came back as In, and motion as Motion, and the character error rate against the printed page is 0.0035 (a MEASURED single run with the Tesseract version named on the slide). The research ran the same page through the three engines the course built or installed and three kinds of English data (the next slides): the first word was Iv with 4.1.1 and with 5.5.3 and the fast data, In with the apt 5.3.4, Ir with the best data of all three, and It with the legacy data under 4.1.1 and 5.5.3. So the sentence the chapter prints, that the output looks like this, is true of one engine and one data set, and the exact text is a property of the version you installed. The corpus program frankensteinPage_v1_0_0.py ran too and is not shown, because its lines are wider than a slide; the program on the slide is cut from it.
slides.take: The exact text is a property of the engine and its data.

slides.notes: Appendix A of the book pins pytesseract==0.3.10 and Pillow==10.4.0. The table is the same probe run under four interpreters when the deck is built: Python 3.14.6 with the newest packages, Python 3.14.6 with the pins, Python 3.13.14 with the pins, and an empty Python 3.14.6. The probe imports pytesseract, reads a drawn line of text and counts the languages. With the pins on 3.14.6 the import raises ImportError, cannot import name 'find_loader' from 'pkgutil', because pytesseract 0.3.10 calls pkgutil.find_loader and Python 3.14 removed it; on 3.13.14 the same pins import and read, and the newest pytesseract, 0.3.13, no longer has find_loader, which the console shows by looking for the name in its source. The empty Python raises ModuleNotFoundError. Tesseract itself does not matter for the failure, because the exception is raised before any text is read. The console needs the packaging module for its last two rows, so it does not run in a Python in a browser unless packaging is installed. The research also recorded that PyPI has 28 releases of pytesseract, that none is numbered 0.3.11 or 0.3.12, and that three older ones, 0.3.4, 0.3.7 and 0.3.8, install only from source; the deck did not run those. Between pytesseract 0.3.9, 0.3.10 and 0.3.13 the only change the research found in one program was the type of the confidence, a str in 0.3.9 and an int from 0.3.10. The Windows and macOS installers of Tesseract, Homebrew, and the final release of Python 3.15 were never used here; the research ran Python 3.15 only as a beta, 3.15.0b4.
slides.take: A pinned release that predates your Python may not import.

slides.notes: The program draws a page of 259 known characters with Pillow, reads it with Tesseract 5.3.4 and prints the character error rate, which is the edit distance between the known text and the result divided by the length of the known text, with every run of white space made one space. Every number is a MEASURED single run, one page, one font, one engine, and not a law. Letters of 6 pixels read at 1.0, which is nothing right; 8 pixels at 0.2394; 10 pixels at 0.0232; 12 pixels at 0.0154; and 24 pixels at 0.0116, which is the floor of this page, one wrong character in the whole text. A page turned by 2 degrees read at 0.0116, by 3 degrees at 0.6409, and by 5 degrees at 0.5328, so a slight tilt is harmless and a few degrees more is not. Noise of standard deviation 40 read at 0.0116 and of 60 at 1.0. White text on a black ground read at 0.0116, which is as good as black on white, because the engine inverts a light-on-dark page by itself (tessedit_do_invert is 1); with that turned off the result is 1.1042, more wrong characters than the text has. So the chapter's advice, dark text on a light ground, describes what the engine did not need here. The numbers in the research package (F9 and F10) were measured on a 700-pixel page and differ in size, for example 0.2278 at 8 pixels there and 0.2394 here; the pattern is the same, and the deck prints the numbers its own program printed. The corpus program whatHurtsAccuracy_v1_0_0.py ran too and is not shown. Ray Kurzweil's machine of 1976 was built because fonts mattered less than size: Fonts stopped mattering, size still does.
slides.take: Size, tilt and noise matter; the engine inverts a dark page itself.

slides.notes: Wikipedia's article on reCAPTCHA says it was acquired by Google in September 2009 and that it helped to digitize the archives of The New York Times and then Google Books. The original service was a mass collaboration platform for digitizing books too illegible for computers. Its prompts used pairs of words from scanned pages, one known word as a control for verification and a second to crowdsource the reading of an uncertain word. In this study Tesseract's own confidence did a small part of that sorting: of the 106 words of frankenstein.png the wrongly read 'In' had confidence 55 against a mean of 94.5. The account rests on these sources. Wikipedia, 'ReCAPTCHA' (acquired by Google in September 2009; pairs of words with one known control word; the archives of The New York Times), read 2026-10-13; this study's leaves LowConfidenceWords and RealWordErrors. The two wrong words of the 106 on Figure 22-1 are IT read as In and motion read as Motion. Both are real English words, so a spell check against the 104,334 words of /usr/share/dict/words flags nothing; the program prints an empty list. The mean confidence is 94.55, and the wrong In has the lowest of all, 55, while Motion has 92, so the low confidence finds one of the two. The picture is the word In enlarged three times with its neighbours, an I followed by a small capital T. The chapter's last step is to give the text to a large language model with a prompt that asks it to fix the mistakes. The research did not run it: no model was called, and the sample prompt in the chapter has 419 characters. What the deck can say is what a program could hand to a model or to a person: the words with a low confidence, and the words a word list does not know. Both lists are short here, which is the point of reCAPTCHA's design, that people are asked only about the words the machine could not read. The deck makes no statement about how well a model would correct the text. The numbers are MEASURED single runs with Tesseract 5.3.4.
slides.take: Real-word mistakes need a confidence or a human, not a spell check.

The text of the pages is what the OCR inside NAPS2 read, and two of the pages were read with a stray character, Spam0O, Spam1l and Spamo6 in this run, so the text of a result is a MEASURED single run and not a given; the page that was picked is what the slices decide. One page of an earlier run of the same program came back empty on its first call and read correctly on three runs after it, a flake of the OCR inside NAPS2 that the deck cannot explain, which is why the program prints the read text and the deck check compares it again each time. The picture shows the seven pages with the three picked by the last slice in red. The Windows, macOS and Flatpak forms of the command were never used here.
